cards.b: 1400s-1500s, Italy first. Realism, linear perspective, anatomy, balance. Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael.
Soft, smoky blending with no hard outlines, used by Leonardo in the Mona Lisa.
Strong contrast of light and dark to create volume and drama.
1600s: drama, movement, rich colour and tenebrism. Caravaggio, Rembrandt, Velázquez.
Very dark shadows lit by a spotlight-like light; typical of Caravaggio.
Late 1700s France. Order, clarity, classical subjects. Jacques-Louis David.
Emotion, imagination, nature and the sublime. Turner, Delacroix, Friedrich, Goya.
Goya, 1814: protest against war and a firing squad; in the Prado.
Mid-1800s France: ordinary people and workers, painted honestly. Courbet, Millet.
1860s-80s France: light, plein air, broken brushstrokes, pure colour. Monet, Renoir, Degas, Morisot.
Painting outdoors, directly from the subject.
Monet, 1872: the painting that gave Impressionism its name.
Artists after Impressionism seeking more feeling, structure or symbolism: Van Gogh, Cézanne, Seurat, Gauguin.
Seurat's technique of tiny dots of pure colour that mix in the viewer's eye.

short.q: Give two features of Renaissance painting and one artist.
short.model: Linear perspective and realistic anatomy/balanced composition; e.g. Leonardo da Vinci.

short.q: How does Post-Impressionism differ from Impressionism?
short.model: Post-Impressionists focused on personal expression, structure or symbolism rather than only capturing light.

short.q: Describe how you could use Caravaggio in a still life study.
short.model: Light the objects with one lamp on dark paper and draw with charcoal and white chalk for strong light and shadow.

short.q: Name one Spanish artist from this period and one work.
short.model: Goya, The Third of May 1808 (or Velázquez, Las Meninas).

short.q: Why is it important to include dates and titles on research pages?
short.model: They show accurate knowledge and context so the work can be identified and analysed.
